_readme: Known wrong mental models for CSW2's prerequisites, each tied to a problem_type.
A wrong answer is only ever matched against misconceptions carrying the SAME
problem_type -- that is what keeps a diagnosis specific instead of generic.
wrong_answer_pattern is a regex matched against the student's answer text, and
it is welded to the wording of the SEEDED practice items below it. Generated
practice uses different wording and different values, so a generated item
carries its own declared option-to-misconception mapping instead -- see
backend/app/services/practice.py. Do not assume a pattern here will match a
generated item. It will not, and that is the whole reason the declared mapping
CONTENT LEAD: every entry should be a mistake you have actually seen a student
make. A plausible-sounding invention produces a diagnosis nobody recognises,
and the student denies it -- which is worse than no diagnosis at all.

misconceptions.label: Treats a class attribute as if every instance had its own copy
misconceptions.description: Assumes a list or dict defined in the class body is created fresh for each object. It is created once and shared, so one instance mutating it changes it for every instance. This is the most common Python bug in student code that works perfectly until a second object exists.

misconceptions.label: Assumes an overridden method still runs the parent's version automatically
misconceptions.description: Expects inheritance to combine the two methods. Overriding replaces; the parent's version runs only if super() is called explicitly, so shared setup silently stops happening and the failure appears somewhere unrelated.

misconceptions.label: Believes a globally installed package is available inside a virtual environment
misconceptions.description: Treats a virtual environment as just a folder rather than as an isolated interpreter with its own site-packages. Produces 'it works on my machine' and requirements.txt files that are quietly incomplete.

misconceptions.label: Assumes the server remembers the previous request without being told
misconceptions.description: Carries an intuition from desktop programs, where state persists between actions. HTTP is stateless: anything the server should remember has to be re-sent, in a cookie, a session, or the request itself.

misconceptions.label: Chooses GET for a request that changes server state
misconceptions.description: Picks the method by convenience rather than by meaning. GET is supposed to be safe and repeatable, so using it to create or delete means a refresh, a prefetch or a crawler can perform the action a second time.

misconceptions.label: Believes an input without a name attribute is still submitted
misconceptions.description: Confuses id, which is for CSS and JavaScript, with name, which is the key the browser actually sends. A field with only an id silently sends nothing, and the bug looks like a server-side problem.

misconceptions.label: Believes URL patterns are matched by specificity rather than in the order listed
misconceptions.description: Expects the router to pick the best match, the way a CSS selector wins by specificity. Patterns are tried top to bottom and the first match wins, so a broad pattern placed early shadows every pattern after it.

misconceptions.label: Chooses a meaningful, changeable value as the primary key
misconceptions.description: Picks something recognisable, like an email address. Real-world identifiers change, and when they do, every foreign key referencing them has to change too.

misconceptions.label: Puts the foreign key on the one side of a one-to-many relationship
misconceptions.description: Reasons that the author owns the posts, so the reference belongs on the author. A single column cannot hold many post ids; the key goes on the many side, which is the row that has exactly one parent.

misconceptions.label: Believes a filter returns a single record rather than a collection
misconceptions.description: Reads filter() as 'find the one that matches'. It returns a collection whose length happens to be one, so calling a field on it fails with an error mentioning the queryset rather than the field, which sends students looking in the wrong place.
